Boston Massacre. It was a violent street confrontation on March 5, 1770, in colonial Boston between British soldiers and an angry crowd of American colonists. Tensions between occupying redcoats and local residents had escalated over months of colonial resistance to parliamentary taxation and trade restrictions. When soldiers fired into the crowd, killing five civilians including Crispus Attucks, the incident became a powerful symbol of British tyranny and accelerated colonial grievances toward independence.

The confrontation occurred in front of the Custom House on King Street, now State Street, during a tense March evening. A crowd of colonists threw snowballs and taunts at a small British guard unit, and soldiers felt threatened. Captain Thomas Preston ordered his men to fire, and seven shots rang out in rapid succession.

Five people were killed. Crispus Attucks, a mixed-race laborer, was shot first and killed instantly, and he is often celebrated as the first casualty of the American Revolution. James Caldwell, Samuel Gray, Samuel Maverick, and Patrick Carr also died, though Carr died later from his injuries. Several others were wounded but survived.

The soldiers were arrested and charged with murder, but were defended by future President John Adams, who secured acquittals for all but two. Those two were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the hand. Patriots seized on the incident to fuel anti-British sentiment. Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty publicized it relentlessly. Paul Revere created a propagandistic engraving depicting soldiers deliberately firing on a defenseless crowd, a distortion that became the enduring image.

The event was commemorated annually on March 5 in Boston. Attucks Street and Massacre Lane mark the site. The Boston Massacre strengthened colonial unity against British rule and vindicated resistance movements ahead of the Revolution. What made it transformative was not the legality but the narrative: patriot organizers crafted a mythology of cold-blooded murder by occupiers on civilians, and despite the legal reality that most soldiers walked free, this mythology proved potent. The massacre became Exhibit A in the case for British cruelty, and in American historical memory, it marks the moment when bloodshed made reconciliation with Britain seem impossible.
